cells.tense: You are at the finish line with the pen in hand, and the work is complete.
cells.ask: Name what finished, tell one person, and leave it alone for a day.
cells.core:
You've been growing something by hand, and it's now at the point where it can stand without you. The finish arrived and it opened rather than closed. That's the sign it's done. The thing you grew has its own life now, and you're free to watch it without holding on.

The risk here isn't failure. It's keeping the old habit running past its purpose — touching the thing to feel useful, mistaking that for care. That's just the next thing wearing the last thing's shape. Letting go of what's finished is not losing it. Name what's done, tell one person, and leave it alone for a day. How cleanly you set this down decides how honestly the next one starts.
cells.sheetLine: Something you grew is finished. Set it down and watch.
cells.verb: apprenticing to the material world — tending something into form and learning its growth by hand
cells.place: the arrival that is also the door, where what is finished releases into what comes next

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future you cannot write yet, pushing the growth ahead of its own pace.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're forcing, pause it for a week, and write what actually happened.
cells.core:
You're getting ahead of the thing you're growing. Imagining the finish, trying to hurry it there, doing the work for a version of events that doesn't exist yet. Care that doesn't trust the pace stops looking like care. The pushing costs you the one thing you'd need most — the room to notice what's actually happening on its own.

What's wanted isn't more pushing. It's the picture coming from what's already happened instead of what hasn't. So pick one thing you're forcing, pause it for a week, and write down what actually happened in that week. That tells you which kind of looking is which.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing a future instead of reading the present.

cells.tense: You are at a door that is already behind you, still deciding whether to lean on it.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing you already began and give it ten minutes today.
cells.core:
Your hands are on something and you're watching it respond. You tend, you notice, you adjust. Ordinary work, alive in the room. That's what it looks like when the hands stay busy and the thing answers back.

Lately the hands are off. What got started sits where you left it. What's empty gets filled by doing, not deciding. Pick one small thing you already began — something with a hand in it — and give it ten minutes today. No plan, no result. Just your hands touching a material world that doesn't need your permission to keep growing.
cells.sheetLine: You started something once. Ten minutes with it today.

cells.tense: You are writing in a room you have already been writing in, pen down, calling it something else.
cells.ask: Look back over the last month, name one thing you grew, and say so plainly.
cells.core:
You've been growing things that are already growing, and you talk about them as if they grew themselves. The work got done, quietly, and the person doing it has been standing off to the side of their own labor. Your hands were in it the whole time. The saying-so hasn't happened.

No one's asking you to take credit for everything. Just to put your hand on the thing you actually made — not the luck, not the timing. The part that was you. Look back over the last month, name one thing you grew, and say so plainly to someone or write it down. Naming it doesn't inflate it. It puts your hand back on the pen.
cells.sheetLine: You grew something this month. Say so.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that the person's past holds a door they are still standing at — Too Little may locate them behind the present but may not say what happened there or what it cost. The reader's likely objection: 'I never apprenticed myself to anything; life just moved.' The ask survives being wrong because it requires only one small ordinary act of attention, which yields information about what holds and what moves even if the read misses. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person: 'You're the one who decides what gets to keep growing' — it flatters the reader rather than handing them anything to do, so I cut it.
